Choose batch, micro-batch or event-driven processing from latency, ordering, replay and state requirements rather than trendiness.
You already know Python, SQL, ingestion, lakehouse fundamentals and Spark batch concepts. This lesson teaches the new
streaming/event behavior from first principles; live Kafka/Structured Streaming operation is never assumed.
Picture two kitchens. One cooks a full day of orders at midnight; the other reacts as each ticket arrives. Streaming is not
simply faster batch - the second kitchen must remember what it already served, handle duplicate tickets, late tickets and
restarts while new work keeps arriving.
5. New words before we use them
Batch: bounded work processed as a set. Stream: unbounded event sequence. Event-driven: work triggered by events. Latency:
delay from event to useful result. State: memory of prior events needed for correctness.

Picture a railway network. A topic is the route, partitions are parallel tracks, brokers are stations holding track segments, and
replicas are backup copies. Ordering is guaranteed along one track, not across every track at once.
5. New words before we use them
Broker: Kafka server. Topic: named event log. Partition: ordered shard of a topic. Offset: position inside one partition. Replica: copy
of a partition. Replication factor: number of copies.

Picture a parcel created at 09:05 but scanned into the system at 09:17. Event time answers when the business event happened;
processing time answers when the system handled it. Late arrival is the gap between those clocks.
5. New words before we use them
Event time: time at source/business event. Processing time: time handled by processor. Ingest time: time received by platform. Late
event: event arriving after newer event-time data. Clock skew: disagreement between clocks.

Protection rule: open only after a saved genuine mastery-check attempt. Read only the scenario you attempted, close this review, then complete a
changed fresh retry and save the new evidence.
Scenario A review
First prove raw rows and unique event IDs separately. Deduplicate on stable event identity, not timestamp alone. Keep
event_time unchanged; compare ingest_time only to classify lateness. A watermark is a state/late-data boundary, not permission
to overwrite source time. Your proof should show raw count, unique-event count, duplicate IDs, maximum lateness,
accepted/dropped late rows and Silver unique-key count.
Scenario B review
Same-checkpoint restart means resume the same logical query/state. A deliberate replay is a separate controlled operation:
bounded source interval, explicit checkpoint identity, deterministic event/business keys and an idempotent sink/upsert. Prove
before/after sink counts and business-key reconciliation; do not call a fresh checkpoint “recovery” if it re-emits already accepted
events without sink protection.
Scenario C review
Adding an optional field can be compatible when consumers tolerate absence. Changing the type of a required field is breaking
unless you explicitly version/transform. Show producer contract, compatibility mode, rejection/quarantine route, consumer
fallback, schema-version monitoring and a rollout/rollback plan.
Scenario D review
Investigate from evidence: source arrival rate → partition distribution → consumer/query input rate → processing rate/batch
duration → watermark/state rows → sink latency/errors. Tuning partitions, state retention or compute before locating the
bottleneck can move or hide the failure. Save the observed metric change that justifies each intervention.

C3-06 MeterStream Protected Gate Review
Protection rule: use only after a saved genuine Gate attempt. Diagnose only your failed competencies, close this review, complete targeted repair,
then save a changed proof. Gate B/C still require explicit assignment from the existing state machine.
Fixture controls your attempt should have discovered
Control
Expected evidence
Raw rows
21
Unique event_id
20
Duplicate event_id
ME005
Raw value sum
295.4
Deduplicated value sum
281.4
Max lateness
89 minutes (ME900)
Schema versions
{'1': 16, '2': 5}
What the controls mean
The raw stream contains 21 rows but only 20 stable event IDs. If the duplicate is not neutralized before business-state
aggregation, the value control is overstated from 281.4 to 295.4. The deliberately late event arrives 89 minutes after event_time.
Your watermark decision must classify that event explicitly; it must not silently rewrite event_time.
Targeted diagnosis
If counts are wrong: inspect event identity/dedup key before windows. If late classification is wrong: print event_time, ingest_time
and watermark boundary. If replay doubles Silver: inspect checkpoint identity and sink merge/business keys. If schema handling
is wrong: show compatibility decision and quarantine/reject route. If lag/state is unstable: separate source backlog, partition
balance, processing rate, watermark/state growth and sink latency.

C3-06 | ASTRA PARITY RC4
FOUR-COURSE SYSTEM • COURSE 3 • DATA ENGINEERING 2026
Page 2
Repair proof
Repair only the failed competency. Save a before/after control table, the changed configuration or code line, and one failure
injection that reproduces the old error. Then rerun the source-to-sink reconciliation.
Repair checklist
Record the failed competency, root cause, smallest safe code/config change, before/after raw and unique controls, checkpoint
identity, replay interval, sink key, observed monitoring evidence, and the exact failure-injection result. Do not mark repair complete
from a code diff alone.
Why the first result looked plausible
Streaming defects often keep the job green while corrupting business state: a duplicate can preserve schema validity, a late row
can land in the wrong window, a new checkpoint can replay old events, and an append sink can double accepted state. Reconcile
business keys and event-time behavior, not merely successful execution.

C3-06 | ASTRA PARITY RC4
FOUR-COURSE SYSTEM • COURSE 3 • DATA ENGINEERING 2026
Page 3
Changed fresh retry
Change event IDs, at least one key/partition distribution, lateness pattern, schema version and checkpoint/replay identifier.
Reattempt without this review open. The retry must produce new observed controls; copying these fixture values is not evidence.
Evidence floor
A pass-quality retry shows: source raw/unique controls; duplicate handling; event-time/watermark classification; checkpoint/replay
behavior; Bronze/Silver reconciliation; lag/query/state/sink monitoring; and a recovery runbook that names the smallest safe
replay/restart scope. Runtime evidence must be from an actually executed runtime or labeled pending.
Explain-back
Explain why your replay is safe, why the watermark matches the business lateness contract, and which evidence would alert an
operator before silent duplicate/loss reaches the trusted sink.
